hosts: Many ornamentals, vegetables, and fruit crops
Common weed hosts can harbor populations during off-season
symptoms: foliage: Tiny yellow or pale spots on upper leaf surface (stippling) Webbing on undersides of leaves under heavy infestations Leaves may turn bronze, curl, and drop prematurely overall_impact: Reduced photosynthesis, stunted growth, lower yield, increased plant stress

description.appearance: Oval, green to yellowish body with two dark spots on the back; eight legs
description.life_cycle: Egg → larva → protonymph → deutonymph → adult; several generations per season
description.notes: Very small, often requires a hand lens or magnification for detection

management: cultural: Maintain adequate irrigation and humidity to reduce stress on plants Remove infested plant debris and weeds Avoid excessive use of broad-spectrum insecticides that disrupt natural predators biological: Introduce predatory mites (e.g., Phytoseiulus persimilis, Neoseiulus californicus) Encourage natural predators such as lady beetles and lacewings chemical: Use miticides (acaricides) as a last resort and rotate chemical classes to avoid resistance Apply to undersides of leaves where mites are concentrated
sources: Helle, W. & Sabelis, M.W. (1985). Spider Mites: Their Biology, Natural Enemies and Control. Elsevier.
Gerson, U., Smiley, R.L., & Ochoa, R. (2003). Mites (Acari) for Pest Control. Blackwell Science.
Jeppson, L.R., Keifer, H.H., & Baker, E.W. (1975). Mites Injurious to Economic Plants. University of California Press.
